rows.themeProjectDescription: Visible-infrared image fusion in low-light environments is a critical technique for robust perception in fields such as surveillance, autonomous driving, and robotics. While visible light sensors provide rich texture details, they suffer from severe performance degradation in low-light conditions; conversely, infrared sensors capture stable thermal radiation information regardless of illumination. This project aims to design and evaluate a unified framework for multi-modal image fusion that effectively integrates the complementary features of these two modalities. The research consists of three key tasks: 1) Developing a fusion network to effectively integrate visible light and infrared image features based on advanced neural network architectures; 2) Conducting extensive performance validation on public datasets using state-of-the-art fusion algorithms as baselines; 3) Applying the fused images to a YOLO-based object detection model, quantifying the performance gains in terms of detection accuracy compared to single-modal inputs, thereby evaluating the practical value of the fusion algorithm for real-world sensing tasks. This research explores how multi-modal fusion enhances scene perception, providing a high-performance solution for night-time security monitoring and intelligent robotic vision.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
High-dimensional signals, such as hyperspectral images, video data, communication channel data, and multidimensional sensing data, naturally contain correlations across spatial, spectral, temporal, and channel dimensions. Directly storing and processing such data may lead to high memory consumption and computational cost. Tensor decomposition provides an effective way to represent multidimensional data with compact latent factors while preserving the main structural information.

This project aims to investigate tensor decomposition methods for multidimensional signal reconstruction and compression. The student will first study classical tensor models, such as Tucker decomposition and CP decomposition, and then implement a basic compression and reconstruction pipeline. Public datasets, such as hyperspectral images, video frames, or multi-channel image data, will be converted into tensor format. The project will evaluate how different tensor ranks influence reconstruction quality, compression ratio, and computational cost.

The main objectives are to build a tensor-based signal processing framework, compare different tensor decomposition models under the same experimental setting, and design quantitative indicators such as RMSE, NMSE, PSNR, SSIM, and compression ratio to evaluate reconstruction performance. If time permits, the student may further explore a simple nonlinear enhancement strategy to improve reconstruction accuracy under limited storage budgets. The expected outcome is a working experimental system, visualized experimental results, and a graduation thesis.

rows.themeTitle: Multidimensional Signal Reconstruction and Compression Based on Tensor Decomposition

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Dense visual understanding in open-world scenarios is an important goal in computer vision. It requires segmentation systems to recognize an ever-growing set of categories over time while maintaining the ability to generalize to unseen classes. Continual open-vocabulary semantic segmentation (COVSS) addresses this need by combining vision-language models with sequential class learning, where a frozen semantic space such as CLIP serves as an external reference for class identity. This paradigm is essential for building practical systems capable of lifelong dense visual understanding.

 

This project aims to investigate how the semantic structure of the vision-language model influences continual learning behavior in open-vocabulary segmentation. There are two main challenges. The first is how to characterize the geometric relationships among class text embeddings in CLIP's semantic space, including inter-class distances, cluster structures, and topological neighborhoods. The second is how to establish quantitative connections between these semantic relationships and the per-class learning dynamics observed during sequential training, including positive transfer to semantically similar old classes, interference between semantically close classes, and forgetting patterns across tasks. Visualization tools, statistical correlation analysis, and controlled task-ordering experiments can be explored to uncover these connections.

 

The expected output should include a semantic visualization toolkit for segmentation class vocabularies, a per-class continual learning analysis framework that tracks individual class performance across sequential tasks, and empirical findings on whether and how CLIP's semantic structure can predict or explain continual learning outcomes such as forgetting and transfer. The analysis can be evaluated through correlation metrics, visual case studies, and comparison across different task orderings.

rows.themeProjectDescription: Hyperspectral images (HSIs) are massive 3D tensors capturing rich spatial and spectral information. However, their enormous data volume poses significant challenges for storage and transmission. While traditional tensor decomposition effectively compresses HSIs by exploiting their low-rank structures, standard decomposition algorithms are computationally expensive and memory-intensive. This project aims to design a fast, lightweight HSI compression and reconstruction pipeline using randomized and sketched tensor algorithms. By applying tensor sketching techniques, the heavy tensor decomposition process is significantly accelerated with a reduced memory footprint. The extracted low-rank factor matrices serve as the compressed representation of the HSI, which are subsequently multiplied to reconstruct the original image.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Low-light image enhancement is an important task in image processing and computer vision. It aims to improve the visibility of images captured under poor illumination while preserving details, colors, and natural appearance. Retinex theory provides an interpretable way to model low-light images by separating illumination and reflectance information. Such a model is useful for understanding and correcting the degradation caused by insufficient light.

 

This project aims to develop a Retinex-inspired low-light enhancement framework. There are two main challenges. The first is how to build a more effective degradation model for low-light images, considering illumination variation, noise, color distortion, and detail loss. The second is how to design a learning-based enhancement network that can combine the interpretability of Retinex modeling with the representation ability of deep neural networks. Optimization-inspired networks, attention mechanisms, or Transformer-based modules can be explored to improve the enhancement performance.

 

The expected system should be able to enhance low-light images automatically and produce visually pleasing results. The performance can be evaluated by both visual comparison and quantitative image quality metrics.

Driven by the surging demand for large-capacity communication and parallel processing, multi-channel broadband chaos sources have attracted increasing attention. As active gain devices exhibiting rich nonlinear properties, reflective semiconductor optical amplifiers (RSOAs) offer a highly promising alternative for parallel broadband chaos generation, particularly when utilized in mutually coupled structures.

In this project, the student will be guided to study the basic theories of RSOA and nonlinear dynamics, and be trained to use VPI photonics and Matlab to simulate the mutually coupled dual-RSOA system.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Media-Based modulation (MBM) was first proposed by Khandani as a new realization of index modulation (IM) for wireless communications, which embedded extra information by creating different channel states with the ON/OFF status of the radio frequency (RF) mirrors around each transmit antenna (TA). Recent studies have focused on the diversity design and detection algorithms for MBM systems. As the secrecy issue becomes significant in wireless networks, more and more researchers try to enhance the secrecy of MBM systems from the perspective of physical layer.

So far, most of the physical layer security (PLS) schemes are designed for time-division duplex (TDD) MBM systems with channel reciprocity. For example, Yildirim, Basar, and Kurt proposed a secure precoder, while Zhang and Zhao found the optimal input probability mass function maximizing the secrecy rate for single-input

multiple-output (SIMO) MBM systems when the channel state information (CSI) of the eavesdropping link is available. When the eavesdropping CSI is not available, different PLS schemes have been designed for TDD MBM systems in many other works. Although frequency-division duplex (FDD) has been widely used in practical wireless communication systems, very few studies have been done on the PLS problem in FDD MBM systems.

Zhou, Gao, and Liao proposed an AN-aided precoding scheme to enhance the security of FDD multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) MBM systems against eavesdropping, and the impact brought by feedback overhead was also analyzed. However, a closed-form solution was not derived in that work, which is often desirable because it can provide explicit analytical insights and reduce computational complexity in system design. Moreover, since abundant channel realizations can be generated in MIMO MBM systems, the feedback amount of MIMO MBM systems is obviously larger than that of conventional MIMO systems. The large amount of feedback in this study caused considerable overhead since all the legitimate channel fading realizations of the down link were fed back by the legitimate receiver.

The main tasks of this project include: (1) By reading relevant literature, become familiar with the basic principles of physical layer security and carefully study existing PLS schemes. (2) Construct a mathematical model of down-link and feedback transmission of FDD MIMO-MBM. (3) Learn the fundamentals of quantized feedback and consider possible ways to apply it to FDD MIMO-MBM systems to reduce feedback overhead. (4) Complete the formula derivation to obtain closed-form solution of the secrecy rate to characterize the secrecy performance of the scheme.

All numerical simulations in this project will be conducted using Matlab. Students who are proficient in Matlab programming and numerical modeling will be easy to finish this work. This research topic originates from cutting-edge advancements of wireless communication, it requires the recruited students spend sufficient energy and time. We welcome like-minded, driven individuals to join us. The students who expect to publish literatures after some practices in our group are sincerely welcome.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Electrooculography (EOG) is a technique that measures the corneo-retinal standing potential of the eye, allowing the detection of eye movements such as saccades, smooth pursuit, and blinks. Compared to video-based eye trackers, EOG is low‑cost, portable, and less affected by lighting conditions or head movements. It has been widely used in human‑computer interaction (HCI) for assistive technologies, hands‑free control, and virtual input systems. However, practical EOG‑based HCI systems must address challenges including signal noise, motion artifacts, real‑time processing, and wireless reliability. This project aims to design a complete wireless EOG acquisition and interaction system, from analog front‑end hardware to a PC‑based interactive application (e.g., a virtual keyboard), demonstrating the feasibility of EOG‑driven HCI with good usability and robustness.


2. Main Task

2.1 Study the characteristics of human EOG signals, investigate EOG acquisition techniques (hardware and software implementations), as well as sensor signal processing methods. Propose and refine the system design, perform component selection, and justify technical solutions.

2.2 Design an EOG acquisition system based on a mainstream analog front‑end (AFE) chip. Implement metal‑electrode‑based EOG signal acquisition and wireless data transmission.

2.3 Develop PC host software to visualise the EOG signal in real time. Design and implement an interactive application based on real‑time EOG signals, such as a virtual keyboard.


3. Expected Outcomes

A physical prototype capable of human EOG signal acquisition and wireless transmission. The prototype shall meet the following technical specifications:

3.1 Signal sampling rate and quality

Sampling rate: ≥ 250 Hz per channel (recommended 500 Hz)

Resolution: ≥ 16‑bit

Common‑mode rejection ratio (CMRR): ≥ 80 dB

Number of channels: ≥ 2.

3.2 Wireless transmission

Support Wi‑Fi (e.g., 2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n)

Data rate: > 1 MB/s (sustained for real‑time streaming)

Packet loss rate: < 1%

3.3 Interactive design

Implement at least one EOG‑based interactive system (e.g., virtual keyboard)

Good demonstration value (e.g., intuitive visual feedback, low latency, robust to unintended blinks)

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Arterial auscultation is a critical non‑invasive technique for assessing cardiovascular health, including blood pressure measurement via Korotkoff sounds, detection of arterial bruits (which may indicate stenosis or aneurysm), and evaluation of peripheral blood flow. Traditional acoustic stethoscopes remain the primary tool for such tasks; however, they suffer from several intrinsic limitations: low sensitivity to low‑frequency arterial signals (typically 20–200 Hz), significant sound attenuation through hollow tubing, susceptibility to ambient noise, and reliance on the examiner’s auditory perception and experience. Moreover, conventional stethoscopes cannot record, store, or quantitatively analyze auscultation signals, hindering telemedicine applications and automated diagnosis.

Recent advances in micro‑electro‑mechanical systems (MEMS) have introduced silicon microphones that offer high sensitivity, flat frequency response down to sub‑Hz ranges, low power consumption, excellent phase consistency, and immunity to radio‑frequency interference. These characteristics make silicon microphones particularly suitable for capturing subtle arterial sound waves through the skin. By integrating a silicon microphone with embedded signal conditioning, wireless transmission, and intelligent software, a modern arterial auscultation system can overcome the drawbacks of traditional stethoscopes. It enables real‑time listening, high‑fidelity recording, remote monitoring, and advanced feature extraction (e.g., Mel‑spectrogram analysis) for objective vascular assessment. This project aims to design and implement such a system, providing a low‑cost, portable, and quantifiable solution for arterial auscultation that can serve both clinical and home‑care scenarios.


2. Main task

2.1 Investigate mainstream electronic stethoscope technologies and their hardware/software implementation methods, as well as arterial sound signal processing techniques. Propose and refine the system design, complete component selection, and conduct solution feasibility studies.

2.2 Design an arterial auscultation hardware system based on a silicon microphone sensor, enabling arterial sound signal acquisition, real‑time headphone playback, and wireless data transmission.

2.3 Design a PC host computer (upper‑computer) software to visualize auscultation signals and extract features.


3. Expected outcomes

Complete a physical prototype of the system that supports arterial sound signal acquisition, real‑time headphone playback, and wireless transmission, with the following technical specifications:

3.1 Sound sampling rate and audio quality:

Sampling rate: ≥ 22.05 kHz (or 44.1 kHz preferred) to adequately capture arterial sounds.

Resolution: 16‑bit ADC per channel.

Signal‑to‑noise ratio (SNR): ≥ 60 dB (A‑weighted).

3.2 Power consumption: Operating current < 20 mA; supports continuous operation for more than 6 hours.

3.3 Wireless transmission: Supports BLE (Bluetooth Low Energy) with data rate > 200 kB/s and packet loss rate < 1%.

3.4 Data processing: Supports Mel‑spectrogram feature analysis.

Project Description:

Network coverage is a fundamental challenge in wireless sensor networks (WSNs), particularly in complex three-dimensional (3D) environments such as underwater monitoring systems. In Underwater Wireless Sensor Networks (UWSNs), reliable sensing performance depends heavily on effective sensor node placement to achieve high volumetric coverage while minimizing uncovered regions and excessive sensing overlap. Unlike conventional 2D deployment models, underwater applications require 3D modeling since sensors operate at different depths and must monitor volumetric regions. This project extends traditional 2D WSN coverage optimization into a 3D underwater deployment environment. The main objective is to model and optimize sensor node placement within a 3D underwater space to maximize volumetric coverage and improve deployment efficiency. The study focuses primarily on geometric coverage optimization rather than detailed underwater acoustic channel modeling. The optimization problem is computationally challenging due to the large search space associated with increasing sensor numbers and possible deployment locations. To address this challenge, the project investigates several well-known nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization techniques, including Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), and Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO). Each algorithm will be comparatively evaluated based on:

1. Volumetric coverage ratio

2. Computational efficiency

3. Solution robustness and stability across multiple simulation runs

Simulation models and 3D visualizations of underwater sensor deployment and coverage performance will be implemented using MATLAB.


Main Tasks:

1. Conduct a literature review on 3D underwater wireless sensor networks (UWSNs), coverage challenges, and nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization algorithms.

2. Develop a 3D simulation model to represent underwater sensor node deployment, incorporating coverage maximization.

3. Implement metaheuristic optimization algorithms (Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Ant Colony Optimization, and Grey Wolf Optimizer) for optimal 3D node placement.

4. Visualize and analyze 3D sensor coverage using MATLAB.

5. Evaluate algorithm performance in terms of coverage rate, computational efficiency, solution robustness, and stability across multiple simulation runs.

6. Conduct a comparative analysis of metaheuristic algorithms to determine the most effective methods for 3D UWSN deployment optimization.

7. Document the simulation development process, algorithm implementation, experimental results, and practical insights for future deployment scenarios.

8. Troubleshoot technical issues systematically using critical thinking and problem-solving skills.


Expected Results/Objectives:

1. Develop a functional 3D simulation model for underwater sensor network deployment and volumetric coverage assessment.

2. Identify the most effective metaheuristic algorithms for optimizing 3D UWSN coverage under realistic constraints.

3. Produce visualizations and analyses demonstrating 3D sensor placement efficiency and coverage performance.

4. Enhance student skills in MATLAB simulation, optimization techniques, 3D data visualization, and collaborative problem-solving.

5. Deliver a comprehensive report summarizing methodology, algorithm comparisons, simulation results, and recommendations for practical 3D UWSN deployment.

Project Description:

Embedded Systems (ES) play an important role in modern applications such as smart homes, environmental monitoring, healthcare devices, industrial automation, and intelligent transportation systems. These systems commonly use sensors to collect real-time environmental data including temperature, humidity, and air quality measurements. This project focuses on developing a real-time embedded monitoring system capable of collecting, transmitting, analyzing, and predicting sensor data behavior. A microcontroller platform (such as a Nucleo or Arduino board) integrated with environmental sensors will be used to acquire real-time data and transmit it wirelessly to a computer using Wi-Fi communication.

The project will combine two complementary analysis approaches:

1- Statistical Process Control (SPC) techniques for monitoring system stability and detecting abnormal behavior.

2- Simple Machine Learning-based polynomial regression models for short-term prediction of future sensor readings.

Students will implement real-time monitoring dashboards, visualize sensor trends, generate SPC charts, and develop prediction models capable of estimating future environmental conditions over short time intervals. A simple alert mechanism may also be developed to notify users when unusual or unstable system behavior is predicted. This project provides hands-on experience in embedded systems, sensor integration, wireless communication, data visualization, and introductory AI-based prediction techniques. It also allows students to explore how traditional statistical monitoring methods can work together with modern data-driven approaches for intelligent real-time decision-making. The project is designed as a guided learning experience, and continuous support will be provided throughout the project duration.


Main Tasks:

1. Conduct a literature review on embedded system monitoring, Statistical Process Control (SPC), and polynomial regression forecasting techniques.

2. Develop a real-time data acquisition system using microcontrollers (e.g., Nucleo or Arduino) and environmental sensors (temperature, humidity, etc.).

3. Implement SPC charts (e.g., X̄-chart) for monitoring real-time system stability and detecting abnormal variations.

4. Build and train polynomial regression models to forecast short-term sensor readings, integrating these predictions with real-time data streams.

5. Develop visualization dashboards overlaying SPC charts with predicted values to assess system behavior and trigger alerts for potential instability.

6. Evaluate system performance by comparing actual sensor data with forecasts and analyzing deviations or patterns.

7. Document the system design, implementation, forecasting methodology, and results in technical reports.

8. Troubleshoot embedded system and modeling issues using critical thinking and systematic problem-solving.


Expected Results/Objectives:

1. Develop a functional embedded system capable of real-time data acquisition and wireless transmission to a personal computer.

2. Implement a hybrid monitoring and forecasting framework combining SPC and polynomial regression for enhanced system reliability.

3. Provide real-time alerts based on predicted instability, improving the system’s decision-support capabilities.

4. Enhance students’ skills in embedded system development, MATLAB data analysis, SPC techniques, and predictive modeling.

5. Deliver visual dashboards and a comprehensive project report summarizing methodology, results, and recommendations for future improvements in embedded system monitoring.

Project Description:

Robot manipulators are widely used in industrial automation, smart manufacturing, and robotic applications where accurate trajectory control is essential. In practical systems, however, small variations in robot joint motions—caused by actuator noise, sensor inaccuracies, or external disturbances—can affect the final movement accuracy of the robotic arm. This project investigates how variations in joint angular velocities influence the trajectory performance of a planar 3-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) robotic manipulator. The main objective is to analyze and visualize the sensitivity of robot trajectories under different operating conditions and parameter variations. To improve computational efficiency, the project will explore data-driven surrogate modeling techniques that can approximate system behavior without requiring excessive repeated simulations. Methods such as Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW), Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation, and other lightweight surrogate modeling approaches will be investigated to accelerate trajectory analysis. Students will develop simulation models and perform comparative analysis to evaluate how surrogate-assisted methods can support faster and more efficient robotic trajectory studies. The project provides hands-on experience in robotic simulation, MATLAB programming, data-driven modeling, and engineering system analysis. The project is designed as a guided learning experience, and continuous support will be provided throughout the project duration.


Main Tasks:

1. Conduct a literature review on 3-DOF planar robot manipulators, trajectory optimization, and uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods.

2. Model the 3-DOF robot manipulator in MATLAB, including forward kinematics.

3. Simulate parametric uncertainty in joint angular velocities and evaluate its impact on end-effector trajectory accuracy.

4. Develop data-driven surrogate models (e.g., Radial Basis Functions) to approximate system responses efficiently.

5. Apply sampling-based uncertainty quantification techniques (e.g., Monte Carlo, Latin Hypercube Sampling) to assess trajectory robustness under realistic perturbations.

6. Visualize and analyze the impact of uncertainty on trajectories, comparing surrogate model predictions with full simulation results.

7. Document simulation models, surrogate modeling methods, experimental results, and analysis of robustness and trajectory deviations.

8. Troubleshoot technical issues systematically using critical thinking and problem-solving skills.


Expected Results/Objectives:

1. Develop a functional simulation model of a 3-DOF planar robot manipulator with joint-space uncertainty.

2. Apply surrogate-based modeling techniques to enable rapid evaluation of trajectory deviations due to parameter perturbations.

3. Quantify the robustness of optimal trajectories under realistic system uncertainties.

4. Generate visualizations demonstrating the impact of uncertainty and surrogate model accuracy on end-effector trajectories.

5. Enhance students’ skills in MATLAB simulation, surrogate modeling, uncertainty quantification, and collaborative problem-solving.

6. Deliver a comprehensive project report summarizing methodology, surrogate model performance, trajectory analysis, and recommendations for robust trajectory design.

Project Description:

Modern antenna design heavily relies on electromagnetic (EM) simulations to evaluate antenna performance characteristics such as reflection coefficient, bandwidth, and radiation patterns. Although full-wave EM simulations provide accurate results, they are often computationally expensive and time-consuming, especially when repeatedly used during antenna parameter optimization. This project investigates the use of data-driven surrogate modeling techniques to accelerate antenna design optimization while reducing computational cost. Surrogate-Based Optimization (SBO) is an intelligent optimization approach in which a fast mathematical approximation model—also known as a surrogate or metamodel—is used to replace expensive simulation evaluations during the optimization process. These surrogate models are closely related to Machine Learning (ML) supervised modeling techniques. The project focuses on optimizing antenna geometry parameters using data-driven surrogate modeling approaches such as Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) and Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation methods. Techniques such as Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) and grid search strategies will also be explored for efficient data generation and parameter exploration. Students will develop simulation and optimization models to evaluate how surrogate-assisted methods can improve antenna performance while significantly reducing optimization time and computational effort. Different surrogate weighting strategies and modeling approaches will be analyzed and compared in terms of prediction accuracy and optimization efficiency. This project provides students with hands-on experience in antenna simulation, optimization, AI-inspired modeling, and computational engineering techniques using MATLAB and related simulation tools. The advisor will provide continuous guidance and support throughout the project.


Main Tasks:

1. Conduct a literature review on antenna design optimization, surrogate modeling techniques, and data-driven optimization approaches.

2. Develop a simulation model using MATLAB Antenna Design Toolbox or CST to analyze antenna geometry parameters and performance characteristics.

3. Learn and apply data-driven surrogate modeling techniques, namely Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation beside Latin Hypercube Sampling (LHS) method for sampling design.

4. Optimize antenna geometry parameters using surrogate-based optimization to improve performance while reducing computational cost.

5. Evaluate optimized antenna designs, comparing surrogate-based optimization results with traditional methods like Genetic Algorithm (GA).

6. Visualize simulation results and optimized designs for clear performance assessment.

7. Document the development process, methodology, optimization procedures, experimental results, and analysis of findings.

8. Troubleshoot technical issues systematically using critical thinking and problem-solving skills.


Expected Results/Outcomes:

2. Apply surrogate-based optimization to enhance antenna performance efficiently while reducing computational effort.

4. Provide comparative insights between surrogate-based and traditional optimization methods.

5. Improve student skills in MATLAB simulation, surrogate modeling, optimization techniques, and collaborative problem-solving.

6. Deliver a comprehensive report detailing the methodology, optimization results, visualizations, and recommendations for future antenna design improvements.

With the global demand for energy conservation, high power density, and system miniaturization, wide-bandgap (WBG) semiconductors have emerged as a foundational technology driving the revolution of power electronic systems, widely applied in electric vehicle (EV) fast charging, renewable energy systems, data center power supplies.Distinguished from traditional silicon-based semiconductors, WBG semiconductors possess superior material properties that enable them to operate stably at higher temperatures (up to around 300 °C) and support device designs with higher blocking voltage capability, addressing the performance bottlenecks of conventional semiconductor devices in harsh working environments and high-power applications.

Targeting this core demand in power electronic system design, this project focuses on the development of universal analytical switching loss models for typical SiC-based half-bridge configurations, which are the basic building blocks of most power converter topologies. Specifically, two universal analytical switching loss models are separately proposed: one for the SiC MOSFET and Schottky diode half-bridge, and another for the SiC MOSFET half-bridge that incorporates temperature-dependent reverse recovery losses of body diodes. Both models are established based on data sheet information, including parasitic parameters that significantly affect switching performance in practical applications, ensuring high accuracy and strong applicability in engineering practice while maintaining computational efficiency. This project provides a reliable technical tool for the optimal design of WBG semiconductor-based power converters, facilitating the widespread application of WBG technologies in high-efficiency, high-power electronic systems.

Project Description:

Wireless Sensor Networks (WSNs) are widely used in applications such as environmental monitoring, smart cities, underwater sensing, industrial automation, and disaster management. One of the major challenges in WSN deployment is achieving effective sensor coverage in complex and irregular environments containing obstacles such as buildings, terrain variations, or natural barriers. In many real-world scenarios, sensors are deployed randomly—using aerial distribution or autonomous systems—which can result in uneven coverage, blind spots, and unnecessary overlap between sensing regions. The presence of obstacles and irregular deployment boundaries makes coverage optimization more challenging, requiring intelligent strategies for sensor placement and network design. This project investigates the use of nature-inspired metaheuristic optimization algorithms, an important subset of Artificial Intelligence (AI), including Genetic Algorithm, Particle Swarm Optimization, Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), and Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO), to improve WSN coverage performance in realistic deployment environments. A comparative study will then be conducted to analyze the performance of the selected optimization algorithms in terms of coverage quality, computational efficiency, robustness, and adaptability to irregular deployment spaces. The performance of each algorithm will be evaluated using standard control performance indices, including Integral of Squared Error (ISE), Integral of Time-weighted Squared Error (ITSE), Integral of Absolute Error (IAE), and Integral of Time-weighted Absolute Error (ITAE). Through comprehensive simulation experiments and performance comparisons across multiple control system models, the project aims to identify the most effective optimization techniques in terms of control accuracy, convergence behavior, robustness, and computational efficiency. Background

Neuromorphic computing, which draws inspiration from the architecture and processing mechanisms of the human brain, has emerged as a promising paradigm to overcome the von Neumann bottleneck in conventional computing systems. At the heart of this technology lies the artificial synapse, a device that emulates the plasticity of biological synapses to enable efficient parallel, event-driven computation. Recently, optoelectronic synapses, which use light as the signal carrier, have attracted significant attention due to their potential for high bandwidth, low crosstalk, and ultrafast operation. Among the material candidates for such devices, perovskite materials stand out owing to their exceptional optoelectronic properties, including high absorption coefficients, long carrier diffusion lengths, tunable bandgaps, and defect tolerance. Furthermore, the unique mixed ionic-electronic conduction in perovskites can be harnessed to realize heterojunction-based devices that closely mimic short-term and long-term synaptic plasticity. The inherent interplay between photogenerated carriers and ion migration in perovskite heterojunctions provides a rich physical mechanism for tuning volatile and non-volatile photoresponses, making them ideal for constructing low-power, multifunctional optoelectronic synapses. This project is situated at the intersection of advanced materials science and neuromorphic engineering, aiming to explore the device physics of perovskite optoelectronic synapses and demonstrate their viability for neural network computation.


Main Task

1. The student is required to undertake a comprehensive study of the fundamentals of perovskite materials, with a specific focus on the working principles of the heterojunction structures that form the core of the synaptic device. This includes understanding charge generation, separation, and transport dynamics at the interface, as well as the key performance indicators such as responsivity, detectivity, response speed, and synaptic weight modulation.

2. The central experimental task involves learning the fabrication processes to prepare perovskite-based optoelectronic synaptic devices. After successful device fabrication, the student will systematically characterize their electrical and optical properties. A critical objective is to test and actively tune the devices’ volatile (short-term plasticity) and non-volatile (long-term potentiation/depression) characteristics by varying the parameters of the incident light pulses—such as intensity, duration, wavelength, and number of pulses—and by applying external bias. This step aims to establish the correlation between operational conditions and synaptic behavior.

3. Based on the experimentally extracted device dynamics, the student will use programming languages like Python to develop a simulation framework. This involves modeling the synaptic behavior and constructing a functional neural network, such as a feedforward or spiking neural network, to perform principle-level cognitive tasks like image recognition or pattern classification, thereby validating the device’s applicability in neuromorphic systems.


Expected Outcome

The anticipated outcomes of this graduation project encompass both hardware realization and software demonstration. On the hardware front, the project is expected to deliver a functional, principle-verifying perovskite optoelectronic synaptic device. Its volatile and non-volatile photoresponse will be thoroughly tested, analyzed, and documented. On the software side, a successful proof-of-concept neural network computation simulation, directly based on the measured characteristics of the fabricated device, will be implemented. This will demonstrate the device’s capability to serve as an artificial synapse for learning and memory tasks. The final deliverables will include a fabricated device sample, the associated simulation code, and a comprehensive written graduation thesis. The thesis will detail the perovskite material properties, device fabrication and characterization procedures, the tunable synaptic plasticity results, the neural network simulation methodology, and a critical analysis of the findings, thereby providing a complete account of the research from material to intelligent computation.

Project Description:

This project focuses on the simulation and optimization of antenna placement in wireless communication systems using the free space propagation model. The model assumes ideal conditions—an environment without obstacles or reflective surfaces—allowing for simplified analysis of signal transmission between a transmitting and a receiving antenna. The aim is to analyze how distance, antenna gain, and signal frequency affect received signal strength, and to evaluate coverage performance over a defined area. A simulation environment will be developed using MATLAB to model signal propagation, visualize coverage, and assess the performance of different antenna configurations. To enhance the effectiveness of antenna deployment, the project will incorporate metaheuristic optimization algorithms such as Genetic Algorithm (GA) or Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). These methods will be used to determine optimal antenna placement strategies that maximize signal coverage or minimize power consumption. This study is relevant for applications in wireless communication planning, sensor networks, and radar systems, and contributes to the broader understanding of signal behavior and system design under ideal propagation conditions.


Expected Student Learning Outcomes:

1. Understanding of electromagnetic wave propagation in free space.

2. Application of mathematical models in antenna placement theory.

3. Simulation and visualization techniques using MATLAB.

4. Introduction to optimization techniques for engineering applications.

5. Experience in analyzing and interpreting signal coverage maps.

6. Applying basic project management skills, including task planning, time management, and progress tracking.

7. Maintaining project logs, writing technical reports, and effectively presenting research outcomes.

8. Collaborating effectively in teams across model development, programming, and data analysis tasks.

9. Addressing technical challenges through analytical thinking and systematic troubleshooting.


Expected Results/Outcomes:

1. Develop a functional MATLAB simulation model that accurately represents free-space signal propagation for antenna placement analysis.

2. Identify optimized antenna placement strategies using metaheuristic algorithms for improved signal coverage or reduced power consumption.

3. Gain insights into the relationship between antenna parameters, signal propagation, and coverage performance.

4. Provide a systematic evaluation and visualization of different antenna deployment scenarios.

5. Enhance student skills in MATLAB simulation, optimization techniques, data analysis, problem-solving, and technical reporting.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
Background


The rapid development of artificial intelligence has led to a surge in demand for efficient hardware acceleration solutions. While general-purpose processors handle control-intensive tasks well, they are often inefficient for compute-intensive neural network workloads. RISC-V, an open-source instruction set architecture, offers a unique opportunity for hardware customization and extensibility. This project aims to design a Neural Processing Unit (NPU) as a coprocessor tailored for neural network calculations, tightly coupled with a RISC-V core. The goal is to offload intensive arithmetic operations from the

main processor to achieve high performance and energy efficiency.


Main Tasks


● Architecture Design: Define the instruction set interface between the RISC-V core and the NPU coprocessor, including custom instructions for loading data, configuring parameters, and triggering computations.

● NPU Micro-architecture Implementation: Design and implement the internal architecture of the NPU, focusing on efficient data paths for matrix multiplication and convolution operations, potentially utilizing DSP and BRAM resources optimally.

● FPGA System Integration: Integrate the RISC-V soft-core processor with the custom NPU design on an FPGA development board, ensuring proper synchronization and data coherence.

● Verification and Testing: Develop testbenches and on-board test programs to validate the functionality of the accelerator using standard neural network models or representative computational kernels.


Expected Outcomes


● A complete Register-Transfer Level (RTL) design of the RISC-V NPU coprocessor system.

● A functional FPGA prototype capable of executing neural network inference tasks under the control of the RISC-V processor.

● Comprehensive performance evaluation metrics, including computational speedup compared to pure software execution, FPGA resource utilization (LUTs, FFs, DSPs, BRAMs), and system latency.

● A comparative analysis of the design's efficiency, demonstrating the advantages of hardware acceleration for specific AI workloads.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Low-altitude airspace (e.g., below 300 meters) has become increasingly congested with unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), drones, and other micro air vehicles. Reliable sensing of these targets is critical for air traffic control, security surveillance, and collision avoidance. Ground-based or infrastructure-mounted sensing base stations equipped with antenna arrays can perform passive or active beamforming to detect, localize, and track low-altitude targets. However, low-altitude sensing faces unique challenges: strong ground/sea clutter, multipath reflections, weak target radar cross-sections (RCS), and the need for real-time, high-precision angle measurement (both azimuth and elevation). Traditional beamforming and angle estimation algorithms (e.g., conventional delay-and-sum, Capon, MUSIC) often assume far-field, line-of-sight conditions, which may degrade severely in low-altitude environments with multipath and interference. This project aims to design dedicated beamforming strategies and novel angle measurement algorithms for low-altitude sensing base stations, ensuring robust detection and accurate angular localization of drones and other low-altitude targets under complex propagation conditions.

2. Main Task

  • Literature review: Review existing beamforming and AoA estimation methods for low-altitude sensing, including clutter suppression techniques (e.g., space-time adaptive processing, STAP) and super-resolution algorithms. Identify gaps: limited work on joint beam-domain processing for both azimuth and elevation, and few real-time solutions suitable for low-cost base stations.
  • System modeling:
  • Model a sensing base station equipped with a uniform planar array (UPA) or uniform linear array (ULA) operating in low-altitude scenarios.
  • Define the signal model including direct path, ground/sea reflections (multipath), and diffuse clutter.
  • Algorithm design:
  • Propose a robust beamforming scheme
  • Develop a high-resolution angle measurement algorithm specifically for low-altitude targets. This may involve:
  • 2D-MUSIC or 2D-ESPRIT for joint azimuth-elevation estimation.
  • Compressive sensing based sparse reconstruction, exploiting the sparsity of target angles in the vertical direction.
  • A deep learning based approach (e.g., a lightweight neural network) for fast AoA estimation under low SNR.
  • Design a processing pipeline: beamspace transformation (to reduce dimension) followed by angle estimation, optionally with recursive tracking for moving targets.
  • Simulation and validation: Implement the proposed algorithms in MATLAB. Simulate various low-altitude scenarios

3. Expected Outcomes

  • A well‑commented MATLAB code package implementing the beamforming and angle measurement modules.
  • A final technical report (40–50 pages) covering theoretical derivations, simulation results, and practical considerations (e.g., array calibration, mutual coupling effects).

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) is the dominant waveform for modern communication systems (e.g., 4G/5G/Wi-Fi) due to its robustness against multipath fading and efficient frequency-domain equalization. Interestingly, OFDM also exhibits excellent properties for radar sensing: its wide bandwidth enables high range resolution, and the subcarrier structure allows flexible waveform design for joint range-Doppler estimation. Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) aims to unify both functions on a common hardware and spectrum resource. Using OFDM as the baseline waveform for ISAC is highly attractive because it is already widely deployed. However, conventional OFDM waveforms designed purely for communication may suffer from poor sensing performance (e.g., high sidelobes in the range-Doppler ambiguity function, power inefficiency for sensing). Conversely, radar-optimized OFDM waveforms may degrade communication bit-error-rate. This project focuses on designing novel OFDM-based ISAC waveforms and associated processing algorithms that jointly optimize communication throughput and sensing accuracy, with particular emphasis on low-complexity receivers and robustness to realistic channel impairments.

2. Main Task

  • Literature review: Survey existing OFDM-based ISAC schemes, including waveform parameter design (subcarrier spacing, guard intervals, pilot patterns), ambiguity function shaping, and joint communication-sensing processing.
  • Waveform and algorithm design:
  • Propose a flexible OFDM waveform parameterization (e.g., subcarrier weighting, null subcarrier insertion, or phase modulation across symbols) that balances communication and sensing performance.
  • Develop a joint optimization framework to minimize the range-Doppler sidelobe level under a communication rate constraint (or maximize rate under a sensing sidelobe constraint).
  • Design efficient processing algorithms at the receiver:
  • For sensing: 2D-FFT based range-Doppler processing, possibly with windowing or sparse recovery methods.
  • Optionally, incorporate adaptive waveform selection based on real-time channel feedback.
  • Simulation and comparison: Implement the proposed waveform and processing chain in MATLAB.

3. Expected Outcomes

  • A well-documented MATLAB/Python code package implementing the waveform generation, transmitter/receiver processing, and performance evaluation.
  • A final technical report (40–50 pages) covering literature review, methodology, numerical results, and recommendations for practical implementation (e.g., consideration of nonlinear amplifiers, phase noise).
  • Potential submission of a conference paper (e.g., IEEE Radar Conference or IEEE ICC) or an extended abstract.

rows.themeProjectDescription:
1. Background

Spatial Modulation (SM) is a promising MIMO transmission technique that conveys information by activating different antenna indices, thereby reducing inter-channel interference and hardware complexity. Meanwhile, Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) has become a core paradigm for future wireless networks, where the same waveform and hardware are shared to achieve both high-rate communication and high-resolution sensing. Conventional ISAC beamforming designs often assume fully digital or hybrid architectures with amplitude/phase control on all antennas, which may be power-hungry and complex. By introducing spatial modulation into ISAC systems, one can exploit the antenna index domain not only for additional information bits but also for flexible beamsteering and sensing pattern control. However, the on–off nature of activated antennas in SM poses new challenges for beamforming design: the beam pattern must maintain low sidelobes and high angular resolution for sensing while ensuring reliable detection of the active antenna indices at the receiver. This project aims to develop novel beamforming and signal processing algorithms tailored for SM-based ISAC systems, enabling efficient joint design of communication and sensing functions.


2. Main Task

  • Literature review: Survey existing works on spatial modulation, hybrid beamforming for ISAC, and joint communication-sensing waveform design.
  • System modeling:
  • Establish a system model for an SM-ISAC downlink scenario: a transmitter with Nt antennas (only one or a subset active per time slot via spatial modulation) serving both a communication receiver (with index detection) and a sensing target (e.g., angle estimation).
  • Define performance metrics: achievable spectral efficiency (bps/Hz) and bit error rate (BER) for communication; beampattern matching error, Cramér–Rao bound (CRB) for direction-of-arrival (DoA) estimation for sensing.
  • Algorithm design:
  • Formulate an optimization problem that jointly designs the activated antenna indices and the analog/digital beamforming weights to minimize sensing beampattern distortion under a communication BER constraint (or maximize communication rate under a sensing CRB constraint).
  • Propose an iterative algorithm combining greedy antenna selection (for SM mapping) and manifold optimization for analog beamforming coefficients.
  • Optionally, design a low-complexity receiver that jointly decodes the spatial symbol and performs sensing parameter extraction.
  • Simulation and validation: Implement the proposed algorithms in MATLAB.


3. Expected Outcomes

  • A well-defined signal model and problem formulation for beamforming design in SM-ISAC systems.
  • A public MATLAB code package implementing the main algorithms and simulation scenarios.
  • A final technical report (40–50pages) covering literature review, methodology, numerical results, and future directions (e.g., extension to massive MIMO with reconfigurable intelligent surfaces).

1. Background

Integrated Sensing and Communication (ISAC) has emerged as a key enabling technology for next-generation wireless networks (e.g., 6G), where the same hardware and spectrum resources are shared to perform both high-data-rate communication and high-resolution sensing (e.g., target detection, localization, and imaging). Hybrid beamforming, which combines a low-dimensional digital precoder with an analog phase-shifter network, offers a cost- and energy-efficient solution for large-scale MIMO systems. However, designing hybrid beamforming for ISAC systems faces challenges: the beamformer must simultaneously satisfy communication metrics (e.g., spectral efficiency, SINR) and sensing requirements (e.g., beampattern matching, Cramér–Rao bound). Most existing works treat the two functions separately or rely on fully digital architectures. This project aims to develop novel hybrid beamforming algorithms that jointly optimize both functionalities under hardware constraints.


2. Main Task

  • Algorithm design:
  • Formulate a multi-objective optimization problem balancing communication and sensing metrics.
  • Propose an iterative algorithm based on alternating minimization or manifold optimization to solve the hybrid precoder/combiner.
  • Optionally, integrate deep unfolding or reinforcement learning for low-latency adaptation.
  • Simulation and analysis: Implement the proposed algorithm in MATLAB.


3. Expected Outcomes

rows.themeProjectDescription:
In modern industrial non-destructive testing (NDT), the accuracy of ultrasonic testing is constrained by the complex parameter combinations of the transmitting board. There exists a highly nonlinear coupling relationship among transmitting parameters such as Voltage, Frequency, Pulse Width, and Gate, Filtering, Backwall Echo, as well as Defect Echo. Conventional fixed-parameter testing methods struggle to cope with signal attenuation and noise interference under complex working conditions (e.g., small-diameter pipes, saddle-shaped welds).

This project aims to establish a mathematical model between the ultrasonic sound field and board parameters, and introduce the Spacetime Echo Potential (STEP) field theory to characterize the acoustic environment. Based on real-time acquired echo data, an intelligent control Agent employing an Actor-Critic architecture will be trained. The agent can dynamically optimize the transmitting board parameters according to the real-time feedback of echo signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and waveform characteristics, thereby achieving accurate defect identification and intelligent compensation, meeting the high demands for automation and intelligence in NDT for high-end manufacturing.
rows.themeTitle: Research and Development of an Intelligent Control Agent for Multi-channel Ultrasonic Testing System
